title: Walking the book
objectives: Compute the average fill price of a market order that eats several levels.
Measure slippage against the best price and against the mid.

screens.prose: A market order buys at once and **walks the book**: it trades level by level until it is done. Each trade is a **fill**. Write down the fills for the order of 1,500 shares.
screens.question: Fill in the shares and the cost at each level.

hints.text: The first two levels are eaten whole. How much is left for the third?
Shares: 500, 600, 400. Cost at each level is shares times price, for example $500 \times 100.14 = 50{,}070$.

feedback.correct: Fills of 500, 600 and 400 shares, costing £150,238 in all.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill level by level, and multiply each fill by its price.

byKey.r2c1: Only 400 shares are still needed when the order reaches £100.18: 1,500 − 500 − 600. It does not take the whole 700.

explain.text: £50,070 + £60,096 + £40,072 = £150,238 for 1,500 shares. The last level is only partly used: 300 shares stay at £100.18.

screens.question: What is the average price per share? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Average price is total cost over total shares.
Divide the £150,238 by 1,500.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the total cost by the number of shares.

byKey.unweighted: £100.16 is the plain average of the three prices (or the answer rounded to the penny). Give four places, from cost over shares.
byKey.best: That is the best ask. Only the first 500 shares paid it.
byKey.last: That is the last price the order reached. Only 400 shares paid it.

explain.text: $150{,}238 / 1{,}500 = 100.1587$. The footer of the book rounds this to the penny, £100.16. Each price counts in proportion to the shares bought there.

screens.prose: The gap between your average price and a reference price is **slippage**. First measure it against the best ask you saw before trading, £100.14.
screens.question: What is the slippage per share against the best ask, in pence?

hints.text: Subtract the best ask from your average price.
£100.1587 − £100.14, then turn pounds into pence.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the average price minus the best ask, in pence.

byKey.last-level: 4p is the worst price minus the best. Most shares paid less than £100.18.
byKey.pounds: That is right in pounds. In pence it is 100 times bigger: 1.87p.
byKey.total: £28 is the total over 1,500 shares. The question asks per share.

explain.text: £100.1587 − £100.14 = £0.0187, or 1.87p a share. Over 1,500 shares that is £28: the price of eating three levels instead of one.

screens.prose: Before you traded, the mid was £100.12. Against the mid you paid half the spread on every share, then the walk on top.
screens.question: How much more did your 1,500 shares cost than 1,500 shares at the mid, in £?

widget.label: Cost against the mid, in pounds

hints.text: At the mid, 1,500 shares would cost $1{,}500 \times 100.12$.
That is £150,180. Compare it with what you paid.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what you paid with 1,500 shares at the mid.

byKey.best-ask: £28 is against the best ask. The mid is 2p lower, which adds £30 more.
byKey.half-only: £30 is the half-spread alone: 2p on 1,500 shares. The walk up the book adds £28.
byKey.per-share: That is per share, in pounds. Multiply by 1,500 shares.

explain.text: £150,238 − £150,180 = £58, about 3.9 bp of the mid. It splits into £30 for the half-spread (2p a share) and £28 for walking the book. The mid is the fairer benchmark, because it does not ignore the spread.

screens.prose: Now someone sends a market buy for 2,000 shares into the same book. The visible asks hold only 500 + 600 + 700 = 1,800 shares.

options.text: Nothing fills, because the book is too small
options.why: A market order fills what it can. The first 1,800 shares trade at once; only the rest is in doubt.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up the shares on offer and compare with the order.

screens.prose: Each time you weighted every price by the shares filled there. With $q_i$ shares filled at price $p_i$: $$\bar{p} = \dfrac{\sum_i q_i \, p_i}{\sum_i q_i}, \qquad \text{slippage} = \bar{p} - \text{reference}$$
screens.question: In this formula, what is $q_i$?

options.text: The shares the order filled at level $i$

options.why: You used the whole level. At the last level only part of the size fills, like 400 of the 700 at £100.18.

options.text: The number of the level, 1, 2 or 3
options.why: The level number only labels the price. The weight is how many shares traded there.

hints.text: At £100.18, did the 1,500-share order use all 700 shares?
The weight at £100.18 was 400, not 700.

feedback.correct: The weights are the fills, not the sizes on show.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about the last level of the 1,500-share order.

explain.text: The weights are what you actually bought at each price. At the last level that is usually less than the size on show, as with 400 of the 700 at £100.18.

screens.title: Walking the book in code
screens.prose: Turn the walk into a function. `asks` is a list of `(price, shares)` pairs, best price first. Take shares level by level until the order is done.
screens.question: Complete `avg_fill(asks, size)`. It returns the average price of a market buy, and raises `ValueError` if the book cannot fill it.

widget.starter:
def avg_fill(asks, size):
    """Average price of a market buy of size shares.

    asks: list of (price, shares), best price first.
    Raise ValueError if the book cannot fill the order.
    """
    left = size
    cost = 0.0
    for price, shares in asks:
        take = ...  # shares bought at this level
        cost += ...
        left -= take
        if left == 0:
            break
    if left > 0:
        ...
    return cost / size


book = [(100.14, 500), (100.16, 600), (100.18, 700)]
print(avg_fill(book, 1500))
widget.solution:
def avg_fill(asks, size):
    """Average price of a market buy of size shares.

    asks: list of (price, shares), best price first.
    Raise ValueError if the book cannot fill the order.
    """
    left = size
    cost = 0.0
    for price, shares in asks:
        take = min(left, shares)  # shares bought at this level
        cost += take * price
        left -= take
        if left == 0:
            break
    if left > 0:
        raise ValueError('not enough shares in the book')
    return cost / size


book = [(100.14, 500), (100.16, 600), (100.18, 700)]
print(avg_fill(book, 1500))
widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests, including an order that fits in the top level, one that empties the book exactly and one that is 1 share too big. Each average is accepted when math.isclose(actual, expected, rel_tol=1e-9).

hints.text: At each level you can take at most what is left of the order, and at most what the level holds.
`take = min(left, shares)`, and that many shares cost `take * price`.
If `left` is still above 0 after the loop, `raise ValueError('not enough shares')`.

feedback.correct: Your function walks the book, weighting each price by its fill.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Compare the first failing test with a walk by hand.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that every `...` is replaced.
byKey.test-1: For 1,500 shares the average is 100.1587. Check that the last level takes only the 400 shares still needed.
byKey.test-6: An order of 1,801 shares is one share bigger than the book. After the loop, raise ValueError when shares are left.

explain.text: `min(left, shares)` is the whole idea: take the level, or what you still need, whichever is smaller. Dividing by `size` only works once every share is filled, which is why the function raises first.

screens.prose: You must buy 10,000 shares, about £1m. In a liquid share 12,000 shares wait at £100.01 against a mid of £100.00, so the order costs £100 more than the mid. This thin share also has a £100.00 mid.
screens.question: How much more than the mid does 10,000 shares of the thin share cost, in £?

widget.label: Cost against the mid, in pounds
widget.accept: £1,800: fills cost £1,001,800 against £1,000,000 at the mid.

hints.text: Walk the asks: how many shares fill at each level?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Walk the asks for 10,000 shares, then compare with 10,000 shares at £100.00.

byKey.half-spread: £500 is the half-spread alone: 5p on 10,000 shares. The walk up four levels costs far more.
byKey.liquid: £100 is the liquid share. The thin share's book is much shallower.
byKey.worst: That prices every share at £100.40. Only the last 2,000 paid that.

explain.text: The fills cost £1,001,800, an average of £100.18, so £1,800 above the mid: 18 bp against 1 bp. In a thin share the size of the order sets the cost. That is why large orders are split into pieces over time, the subject of level 2.

ideas: A market order walks the book: it takes the best level, then the next, until it is filled.
The average fill price weights each price by the shares filled there, not by the size on show.
Slippage against the mid is half the spread plus the walk; an order bigger than the book cannot fully fill.

quiz.prose: Asks: 500 at £100.14, 600 at £100.16, 700 at £100.18. Trader X buys 1,500 shares in one market order. Trader Y buys 500 at a time, three times, and the book refills to the same prices between orders.
quiz.question: Who pays the lower average price?

X, because one order pays the spread only once
options.why: Each of Y's orders pays the same half-spread per share. X pays more because the big order walks up to £100.18.

options.text: Both pay the same: they buy the same shares
options.why: X's single order eats three levels. Y's small orders never leave the top level.

feedback.correct: Small pieces stay at the best ask.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how far up the book each order walks.

explain.text: X averages £100.1587; Y pays £100.14 every time, saving £28. Real books do not refill for free, so splitting has its own costs. Level 2 weighs them.
